_meta.title: Περιπατητικοί — the heads of Aristotle's Lyceum, 335 BCE – c. 200 CE
_meta.note: Succession order, headship dates, and birthplaces after the project infographic. 'heads' are the eight known scholarchs of the Lyceum (335 – c. 86 BCE). 'later' are Peripatetics active after Sulla's sack of Athens (86 BCE) whom later writers sometimes count as heads, down to the imperial chair held by Alexander of Aphrodisias.
_meta.unplotted: Erymneus (no. 8) has no recorded birthplace and is not mapped.
_meta.sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives, Book 5; Strabo; Ammonius; Smith, Dictionary of Greek and Roman Biography; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.

heads.name: Aristotle
heads.bio: Founded the Lyceum around 335 BCE after years tutoring Alexander of Macedon. His school, the Peripatos, pursued the whole span of knowledge — logic, physics, biology, ethics, politics, poetics — and his surviving treatises shaped philosophy and science for two millennia.

heads.name: Theophrastus
heads.bio: Aristotle's closest pupil and chosen successor, who led the Lyceum for some thirty-five years and is said to have taught two thousand students. His botanical works founded the study of plants, and his Characters sketched human types with dry wit.

heads.name: Strato of Lampsacus
heads.bio: Called 'the Physicist' for his devotion to natural science. He pushed the school toward a thoroughgoing naturalism, explaining the cosmos by inherent forces rather than divine design, and tutored the future Ptolemy II at Alexandria.

heads.name: Lyco of Troas
heads.bio: Led the Lyceum for over forty years, admired for a polished eloquence that gave the Peripatos social standing in Athens, though later critics felt his style outran his substance.
heads.note: Diogenes Laertius says 'of the Troad,' usually taken as Alexandria Troas.

heads.name: Aristo of Ceos
heads.bio: Succeeded Lyco and wrote biographies and ethical works in the Peripatetic manner; several of his character sketches survive through later quotation.
heads.note: Strabo names Ioulis on Ceos as his home.

heads.name: Critolaus
heads.bio: A defender of Aristotelian doctrine against the Stoics. In 155 BCE he joined Carneades and Diogenes on the famous philosophers' embassy from Athens to Rome, where their lectures electrified and alarmed the Roman elite.
heads.note: Head by 155 BCE, when he joined the Athenian embassy to Rome.

heads.name: Diodorus of Tyre
heads.bio: Pupil and successor of Critolaus, who blended Peripatetic ethics with a Stoic tinge, holding the highest good to combine virtue with freedom from pain.

heads.name: Erymneus
heads.bio: A head of the Lyceum around 110 BCE, known only from a passing mention in Athenaeus. His birthplace is not recorded.

later.name: Andronicus of Rhodes
later.bio: The editor who gave Aristotle's school treatises the arrangement we still use, rescuing them from neglect. Ammonius calls him the eleventh head, but he taught at Rome rather than in an institutional Lyceum at Athens.

later.name: Boethus of Sidon
later.bio: Andronicus' pupil and a sharp commentator on Aristotle's Categories and Physics. Some later writers also call him the eleventh head of the school.

later.name: Cratippus of Pergamon
later.bio: A leading Peripatetic of the late Republic who taught Cicero's son in Athens; Cicero thought him the foremost of his school. Whether he formally headed the Lyceum is uncertain.

later.name: Alexander of Aphrodisias
later.bio: The greatest ancient commentator on Aristotle, 'the Exegete,' who held the imperial chair of Peripatetic philosophy at Athens — a headship confirmed by inscription. His commentaries shaped how Aristotle was read ever after.
